deep.reconstruction:
This folio is a draft of the introductory part of Riemann's posthumously published fragment 'Mechanik des Ohres' (ed. Henle, Zeitschrift für rationelle Medicin, 3. Reihe, Bd. 29, 1867; reprinted in the Gesammelte Werke). The next page (p.1, on method in sense-organ physiology) belongs to the same fragment. The page contains no computation, only one small piece of mathematical modelling.

(a) Top block, later separated off by a rule. The ear's task is to transmit the effect of the air's pressure changes to the labyrinth water as unweakened as possible.

(b) 'p.10' block. It has long been recognised that the middle-ear apparatus (Paukenhöhle) transmits air pressure to the labyrinth water in amplified form. The conditions this transmission must satisfy are to be inferred from the ear's observed performance. That performance is chiefly its fineness in distinguishing Klang (timbre) and the acuity of the trained ear.

Riemann defines Klang as the property of a sound that is independent of its strength and direction. The apparatus reproduces Klang perfectly if it transmits the pressure change at every instant amplified by a constant factor. In modern notation, with p_a(t) the air pressure and p_w(t) the labyrinth-water pressure:

  dp_w/dt = k * dp_a/dt, with k constant.

(c) Mathematical expression for Klang. Let v(t) = dp/dt. The curve v(t) determines the sound wave completely except for its direction. Strength enters as a multiplicative factor: v -> c*v. Riemann therefore takes L(t) = log v(t), so that

  log(c*v(t)) = log c + log v(t).

Scaling the strength only shifts the curve vertically. The differences of ordinates, L(t1) - L(t2), are therefore independent of strength and characterise Klang completely. The time-shift invariance is implicit: these are curve 'shapes'. The claim that ordinate differences are invariant is my explicit restatement of his phrase 'Unterschiede deren Ordinaten'.

(d) Application. If the apparatus worked perfectly, the Klang curves of the air and of the labyrinth water would coincide exactly. Experience, namely the fineness of perceiving e.g. small differences of pronunciation, only justifies a weaker assumption: the curve is changed very little. Equivalently, the ratio

  r(t) = (dp_w/dt)/(dp_a/dt)

stays nearly constant over short times.

A slow variation of r(t) remains compatible with this. It would only alter perceived loudness, about which experience does not decide. If the Klang curve were really altered, the observed fineness would be hardly explicable. Riemann concedes that judging this fineness remains subjective.
errors: log of dp/dt is undefined where the pressure velocity is negative or zero. Strictly one needs log|dp/dt| together with the sign function, or a ratio of ordinates. Riemann does not address this; it is a minor imprecision, not a substantive error.
Calling the log-curve's form 'independent of strength' is exact only modulo vertical translation (log c). Riemann himself refers to ordinate differences, so this is consistent.

results.what: Condition for faithful timbre transmission: the middle ear must transmit the pressure rate dp/dt at each instant with a constant (amplifying) factor.
results.modern_name: Linear, distortion-free transmission with constant gain (impedance-matching / transformer function of the middle ear)
results.usually_credited_to: Amplification idea: Helmholtz (1868) and earlier physiologists. Riemann's own formulation appears in 'Mechanik des Ohres' (1867).

results.what: Representation of Klang by the logarithm of the pressure-velocity curve, so that loudness scaling becomes an additive vertical shift.
results.modern_name: Log-amplitude (gain-invariant) signal representation; scale invariance via logarithm

results.what: Fineness of timbre perception implies the ratio of simultaneous pressure changes is nearly constant; slow variation is permitted, affecting only loudness.
results.modern_name: Slowly varying gain / quasi-stationary linear system

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of passages from Riemann's 'Mechanik des Ohres', which Henle published in 1867 and which appears in the Gesammelte Werke. The mathematics, scale invariance under a logarithm, is elementary.

checkable.asserts: Scaling the velocity by a strength factor c shifts its logarithm by the constant log c (for positive c and v).
Differences of ordinates of the log-curve are independent of the strength factor c.
If the water pressure is k times the air pressure (k constant), the ratio of their rates of change is constantly k.

transcription_corrections: The phrase after 'Unterscheidung des Klanges' plausibly reads 'Unterscheidung der Klangfarbe' or 'des Klanges'; it is uncertain in the image.

'Die Curve, welche die Geschwindigkeit der Druckänderung als Function der Zeit darstellt, bestimmt die Schallwelle vollständig bis auf ihre Richtung' is the sense of the passage. 'bestimmt' is partly obscured in the machine transcription.
Near the bottom, 'ist darum sehr wohl vereinbar' should probably read 'ist damit sehr wohl vereinbar' (likely, uncertain).
'Ueber den ... Bedingungen' is corrected in the manuscript to 'Unter den oben aufgestellten Bedingungen ...'; the beginning of that line reads 'Wie[?] den oben ...' rather than 'Ueber'.
